A voice is the one instrument everyone knows the sound of: a vocal that's boomy, popping, hissing or
boxy is heard at once. Most of the fixes are in where the mic goes, before any plug-in.

## Which mic, for the room you have

- **Large-diaphragm condenser**, 15–25 cm away: the studio sound, open and detailed. It also hears the
  room, so it needs a quiet, **treated** room (or a well-made vocal booth).
- **Dynamic** (SM7B, SM58 type), close (2–8 cm): hears much less of the room. The better choice in an
  ordinary bedroom, for loud singers, and on stage. Many famous vocals were recorded on one.
- Whichever you use, it's a **cardioid**: point its dead back at the noisy things (the computer, a
  window, the headphones' spill) ([Recording 2: Polar patterns](rec-mics.qmd#polar-patterns)).

## Distance

Close is intimate and bass-heavy (the **proximity effect**), and every lip noise is there; further back
is more natural and has more room in it. A singer who moves changes the level and the tone: keep a
fixed distance (a hand's width is a handy measure with a condenser), or move on purpose, back for loud
notes, in for quiet ones ([Recording 3: Distance](rec-placement.qmd#distance)).

## Pops and esses

<div class="gear-fig" data-fig="vocal-setup"></div>

- **Plosives** (p, b, and some t, d, k) push a jet of air straight out of the mouth, a little downward.
  A mic in that jet gets a thump of wind that no EQ removes cleanly. A **pop filter** (mesh or metal,
  5–10 cm from the mouth) stops it. So does moving the mic **out of the jet**: a little above the mouth,
  pointing down at it, or slightly to the side.
- **Sibilance** (s, sh) is high and beams forward. A mic slightly above or to the side hears less of it.
  A bright condenser makes it worse; a de-esser in the mix is the last resort.

Drag the mic around the singer. Listen to the "p" at the start of each phrase and the "s" in the middle,
then try the pop filter, the dynamic, and the three rooms:

<div class="rk" data-w="vocalmic"></div>

## Height and angle

Start at mouth height or a little above, 15–20 cm away for a condenser, pointing at the mouth. Pointing
at the nose gives more nasal sound; at the chest, more chest. Have the singer stand as they'll sing:
a lyric sheet on a stand below the mic makes them look down and sing into the floor. Put it at eye height.

## The room

A condenser in a bare room records the room: a **boxy**, hollow sound from reflections close behind and
beside the singer. The walls behind the **singer** matter most (that's where the mic's front points).
A duvet or thick blanket hung behind the singer, a wardrobe full of clothes, rugs on the floor: all
help. Foam squares on the wall only take the top off. A dynamic close up hears much less of it.

## Headphones, level and takes

- **Closed-back headphones**, not too loud: their spill gets into a sensitive mic ([Recording 6: Monitoring](rec-monitoring.qmd)).
- Set the level on the **loudest** part of the song, with headroom ([Recording 1: Gain Staging](rec-gain-staging.qmd)).
- Record several takes; singers warm up as they go (the [Vocal Warm-up](../tools/vocal-warmup.qmd) first).

## On stage

A handheld dynamic, close: lips a finger or two from the grille. Hold it by the **handle**, never the
grille (cupping it turns it omni and it feeds back: [Recording 2](rec-mics.qmd#dont-cup-the-mic)). Keep
its back toward the wedge monitor, and back off on loud notes ([Pop Singing: the mic](voice-pop.qmd)).
